title: Intermittency Mosaic: Latency-Cost Brief
content:
Purpose:
This note describes a small, focused experiment and analysis we ran to study how intermittent request patterns (high variance in per-session token counts and burstiness within sessions) change the tradeoffs between latency SLOs and token unit cost. The goal is to produce an "intermittency mosaic" — a compact textual representation that captures how percentile latency and effective cost per 1M tokens shift across three operational configurations.

Executive summary (short):
- Intermittency hurts P99 far more than median; P99 increases by ~2.8–4.5x depending on config when moving from steady low-variance traffic to high-variance sessions.
- Cost-optimized stacks (aggressive quantization + larger batching windows) cut unit cost by ~35–45% on average but amplify tail latency under high intermittency.
- A hybrid approach (warm pool + per-session KV affinity) buys ~55–70% of the cost benefit while keeping P99 within 1.6x of low-variance baseline.
- Recommendation: expose an "intermittency index" signal to routing and autoscaler so routing policies can pick the appropriate tradeoff per-customer SLO.

Methodology (short):
- Workloads: three synthetic session mixes composed from trace sampling of internal synthetic-client:
  1) steady-30: sessions with 30 tokens median, small variance (sigma ~8).
  2) mixed-episodic: 80% short (5–20 tokens), 20% long tails (200–1200 tokens).
  3) high-intermittency: session arrivals bursty (Poisson bursts) and per-session tokens heavy-tailed (Pareto alpha=1.8).
- Models: two model variants we commonly run in production: rwi-13B-fp16 (baseline) and rwi-13B-8bit (quantized optimized).
- Hardware: single-A100-80GB per serving instance and a dedicated prewarm pool (10% capacity) where used.
- Configurations tested (three):
  A) Low-latency (LL): prewarm pool, small batch window (max latency 10ms), conservative quantization (fp16).
  B) Cost-optimized (CO): aggressive batching (window 80ms), rwi-13B-8bit, no warm pool.
  C) Hybrid-mosaic (HM): moderate batching (40ms), rwi-13B-8bit, small warm pool and per-session KV affinity.
- Metrics captured: median, p95, p99 latency (ms), cold-start fraction, tokens served, cost per 1M tokens (USD, inclusive of amortized warm pool), and effective throughput.

Results (annotated tables in text):
Latency percentiles (ms) by workload and config:

| Workload        | Config | median | p95  | p99  | cold% |
|-----------------|--------|--------|------|------|-------|
| steady-30       | LL     | 21     | 46   | 82   | 0.8   |
| steady-30       | CO     | 34     | 88   | 130  | 3.2   |
| steady-30       | HM     | 25     | 54   | 95   | 1.1   |
| mixed-episodic  | LL     | 28     | 120  | 210  | 4.0   |
| mixed-episodic  | CO     | 56     | 300  | 470  | 9.8   |
| mixed-episodic  | HM     | 40     | 150  | 245  | 5.1   |
| high-intermittency | LL  | 45     | 310  | 680  | 12.5  |
| high-intermittency | CO  | 90     | 720  | 1210 | 27.6  |
| high-intermittency | HM  | 60     | 360  | 830  | 14.2  |

Observations from the table above (textual):
- The CO stack reduces median latency in some steady cases because batching boosts throughput efficiency, but for bursty, long-tail sessions CO chews the tail — p99 is the worst-case offender.
- Cold-start fraction correlates strongly with p99; the CO config's higher cold% explains a large portion of the p99 delta under intermittent patterns.

Cost per 1M tokens (USD, amortized):

| Workload        | Config | cost_per_1M_tokens |
|-----------------|--------|--------------------|
| steady-30       | LL     | 185                |
| steady-30       | CO     | 110                |
| steady-30       | HM     | 125                |
| mixed-episodic  | LL     | 202                |
| mixed-episodic  | CO     | 130                |
| mixed-episodic  | HM     | 145                |
| high-intermittency | LL  | 230                |
| high-intermittency | CO  | 150                |
| high-intermittency | HM  | 165                |

Interpretation (text bullets):
- CO yields the lowest unit cost in every workload but at the expense of tail latency risk. The biggest relative savings appear for steady traffic (~40% lower than LL).
- High intermittency increases unit cost across all configs because inefficiencies from cold starts and smaller effective batch sizes reduce throughput utilization. The delta is largest for LL -> HM/CO transitions where warm pool amortization matters.

Intermittency index (proposed):
- We defined a small, synthetic "intermittency index" (II) to summarize trace behavior for routing/policy decisions. II = (CV_session_tokens * burst_factor), where CV_session_tokens is coefficient of variation of tokens/session and burst_factor is the fraction of request-time windows in which arrival rate > 3x baseline.
- Rough buckets: II < 1.0 (steady), 1.0–3.0 (mixed), >3.0 (high-intermittency). For our traces the three workloads map to II = 0.6, 1.9, 4.6 respectively.
- We simulated a simple routing policy that selects CO if II < 1.0, HM if 1.0 <= II <= 3.0, and LL for II > 3.0. This policy reduced expected cost by ~18% vs always-LL and kept p99 increases to <1.8x baseline for mixed/high cases.

Textual "chart" (mosaic view):
- Each row below is a workload; columns are Configs LL | HM | CO. Within each cell we show: median / p99 (ms) — $cost_per_1M (USD) — cold%. Use short indicators: G (green: p99 < 2x baseline), Y (yellow: p99 2–3x), R (red: p99 >3x).

steady-30:  LL: 21/82ms — $185 — 0.8% (G)  |  HM: 25/95ms — $125 — 1.1% (G)  |  CO: 34/130ms — $110 — 3.2% (G)
mixed-episodic: LL: 28/210ms — $202 — 4.0% (Y) | HM: 40/245ms — $145 — 5.1% (Y) | CO: 56/470ms — $130 — 9.8% (R)
high-intermittency: LL: 45/680ms — $230 — 12.5% (R) | HM: 60/830ms — $165 — 14.2% (Y) | CO: 90/1210ms — $150 — 27.6% (R)

Key recommendations (actionable):
- Add III (intermittency index) telemetry to ingress and make it available to the routing decision path. Start with a 24h rolling II and a 10m short-term II for autoscaler triggers.
- Expose a per-customer routing knob (prefer_cost vs prefer_latency) and default it via a policy that uses II buckets.
- For high-II customers prefer warm-pool + KV affinity (HM) as a balanced default; for low-II prefer CO to save cost.
- For billing/console: surface the II and show a forecasted cost vs p99 curve if they toggle preference.
- Follow-up experiments: test HM with a slightly larger warm pool (20%) and an adaptive batching window that shrinks during detected bursts.

Notes, caveats, and open questions:
- Synthetic traces are derived from sampled production-like shapes but not actual customer PII traces; results should be validated on a per-customer basis before setting contracts/SLA.
- We used rwi-13B variants; results will change for larger models where KV cache memory and attention complexity shift the queueing dynamics.
- The cold% metric was sensitive to warm pool sizing and to placement of KV cache affinity.

Next steps:
- (JIRA-OBS-412) Instrument II at the edge and run a one-week A/B where 5% of traffic gets II-driven routing to validate cost/p99 drift on real traffic.
- Implement a console visualization (mosaic) that lets customers preview tradeoffs interactively.
- Draft a short customer-facing note describing II and recommended defaults for hosted vs dedicated customers.

Appendix: quick reproduction notes (for engineers) — commands and seeds:
- Trace synth: tools/trace-synth --seed 20260401 --shape mixed-episodic --duration 3h --out /tmp/mixed-episodic.json
- Perf harness: bench/perf-run --model rwi-13B-8bit --instances 24 --batch-window 80ms --warm-pool 0.0 --trace /tmp/mixed-episodic.json --out /tmp/bench-co.json
- Cost calc: tools/cost-calc --usage /tmp/bench-co.json --amortize-warmpool 10 --currency USD

End of brief.
